title: Be a mensch (Avot 2:5)
hookLine: Hillel: where there are no decent people, strive to be one

cards: A man drops a bag of groceries on a busy sidewalk. Oranges roll everywhere. Twenty people see it.
They slow down, look, and keep walking, because surely somebody else will help. Then one person stops, crouches down, and starts picking up oranges. Suddenly two more people stop too.
If you've spent any time around Jewish grandparents, you have a word for that first person: mensch. And the idea goes back to one line of Hillel.

teach.b: Mensch is Yiddish, from the German word for a human being. In Yiddish it grew into something more: a person of integrity, decent, kind and trustworthy, someone who does the right thing without being asked.

Calling someone a real mensch is one of the highest compliments there is, and it has nothing to do with money, fame or cleverness. In Pirkei Avot, Hillel gives a short list of who can and can't do what.
A person who's too bashful can't learn, because they won't ask questions. A person who's short-tempered can't teach.

teach.h: WHERE NO ONE IS, BE SOMEONE.
teach.b: Then his final line: in a place where there are no people, try to be a person. The Hebrew for person there is ish, and it clearly means more than just being human. It means someone who stands up.
When nobody is stepping forward, you step forward. When nobody is being decent, you be the decent one. Commentators read it a couple of ways.
The plain way: when no one else is taking responsibility, take it. Another: even where there's no one around to see you, still act like a real person. Either way, Hillel's word is strive.
It isn't easy to be the first one to stop on the sidewalk; everyone else walking on pulls on you.
Being a mensch means feeling that pull and crouching down anyway. And once one person does, others often follow.

how: Calling someone a mensch is a common Jewish compliment for integrity and kindness, and parents and teachers often quote Hillel's line when urging children to do the decent thing.

o: a successful man who has made his family proud
a decent person who does right without being asked
a wise scholar who knows the law by heart

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: mensch comes from the German word for a human being
in Yiddish it grew to mean a person of integrity.
Hillel says the bashful make the best students
he says the bashful can't learn, because they won't ask.
being a mensch is about being clever or successful
it's about decency: doing the right thing when others don't.

games.q: a man drops his groceries on a busy sidewalk. everyone slows down and keeps walking. what do you do?
o: keep walking. someone else will help.
stop and start picking up oranges.
film it. it's kind of funny.
games.why: Hillel: in a place where there are no people, strive to be a person. once one person stops, others often follow.

practice: Think of a place you'll be today, a meeting, a family chat, a train, a classroom, where something goes undone because everyone waits for someone else: the dishes after dinner, the new person nobody talks to, the joke that goes too far.
Picture yourself being the one who moves first, just once, and feel what that's like.

wordCard.voice: Mensch. Yiddish for a human being, and for a decent one. Hillel said: in a place where there are no people, strive to be a person.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: strive to be a person. Yiddish speakers would say mensch.

carryVoice: Your line: crouch down anyway. Ish, mensch: a person in the full sense. Two hundred fifty-four days in.
